case_study_insert.main_stem: Sunridge Citrus Ranch (SCR) is a partnership in the citrus-growing and fresh-produce sector, employing a workforce of 30. Founded in 2011 by Elena Sunridge, it supplies fresh citrus to national fruit wholesalers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. SCR plans to invest $540,000 in a new packing and cold-storage shed, financed by a $300,000 ten-year bank loan and $240,000 of retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 50,000 units a year for its wholesalers. SCR faces two problems: a blemish defect rate of 3.3% and labour turnover of 11%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Market Report — Q3 2025: The ranch packed 12,500 units last quarter at a blemish rate of 3.3%, down from 4.8% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 29 to 15 a month. Average delivery to wholesalers is 3.6 days. A survey of 400 buyers found that 72% would pay up to $0.30 more for locally grown citrus and 58% check origin labels. Training records show 9 of 30 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new grading line; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sunridge Citrus Ranch as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, lifting the cost of variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.80 to $13.71 an hour from April 2026, increasing wage costs. (3) Fertiliser and packaging input costs have increased 10.2% year-on-year, food-price inflation is 5.9% and consumer spending on fresh citrus grew 3.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: SCR plans to fund part of its packing-shed expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCR of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit of $240,000 requires no interest or repayment, so the partnership avoids increasing debt service on top of the $300,000 bank loan while meeting fixed costs of $180,000 a year. The saving can fund better grading to tackle the 3.3% blemish rate and protects the $6.00 contribution on each of 50,000 units sold to wholesalers.

Point 2: Using retained profit avoids lender conditions and keeps control with founder Elena Sunridge and the partners. If the 11% labour turnover held back the harvest, a bank could seek repayment or security over the new shed, endangering the $540,000 project; internally generated cash has no such risk. Retained profit can also be deployed immediately for the 9 of 30 staff needing training, unlike a loan whose drawdown depends on approval, and it leaves the existing $300,000 facility untouched for seasonal working capital.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SCR's $240,000 retained profit, loan, defects and turnover.

questions.question_text: SCR is promoting its new locally grown citrus range. Consider a national television campaign, local radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SCR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: Television could rapidly create awareness of locally grown citrus among millions of shoppers nation-wide. For a 30-worker partnership facing $180,000 fixed costs, however, airtime and production are expensive and a large fraction of viewers buy no fresh citrus or are beyond the wholesaler network, making much of the spend wasteful. It would also compete with repayments on the $300,000 loan used for the $540,000 shed.

Local radio sponsorship: Regional radio is cheap and reaches the communities near SCR's orchards, and it suits a short seasonal campaign. Its weakness is coverage: SCR supplies national fruit wholesalers and must move 50,000 units a year, so local listeners alone cannot drive enough volume, and radio cannot show the fruit's appearance or origin labels.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and lifestyle influencers can show the origin story to the 72% of 400 surveyed buyers who would pay $0.30 more for locally grown citrus and the 58% checking origin labels, at low cost per reached buyer with measurable responses. Results take time to build and depend on influencer trust, but the match to the research is strong.

Recommendation: SCR should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the identified buyers nationally, costs far less than television and supports the premium underpinning the $6.00 contribution per unit. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted; radio is rejected because its reach is too narrow for national wholesale contracts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited SCR context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in SCR's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends influencer marketing, explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: SCR's blemish defect rate is 3.3% and labour turnover is 11%. Explain two benefits for SCR of using a bonus scheme to motivate its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bonus linked to fewer blemished fruit gives the 30 workers a direct financial incentive to handle citrus carefully, which can reduce the 3.3% blemish rate now seen on the grading line. Better quality protects the $11.00 selling price with wholesalers and the $6.00 contribution on each of 50,000 units, so a bonus that cuts waste pays for itself through higher saleable output rather than adding to the $180,000 fixed costs.

Point 2: A bonus can improve retention by rewarding staff who stay through the harvest, addressing the 11% labour turnover that forces repeated induction of the 9 of 30 workers needing on-the-job training at $700 a head for college courses. With laissez-faire leadership and a flat structure, a clear bonus target also gives employees direction that a hands-off style may lack, stabilising the team while the $540,000 packing shed is commissioned.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of a bonus scheme (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SCR's 3.3% defects, 11% turnover and training.

questions.question_text: SCR must upskill 9 staff to operate the new grading line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should SCR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching beside the grading line is tailored to SCR's own equipment and quality standards, has no fees and keeps the 9 trainees working while they learn, protecting the 12,500 units packed last quarter and the reduction of blemishes from 4.8% to 3.3%. Drawbacks are that mentors are working staff whose own tasks suffer, errors during practice could raise the 3.3% defect rate, and no external certificate is awarded, which some wholesalers may expect.

Off-the-job training: A college course at $700 per employee costs $6,300 for 9 staff, easily affordable beside the $540,000 investment, and delivers structured knowledge with a recognised qualification. However, taking 9 of 30 workers off the line reduces capacity during packing and may aggravate the 11% labour-turnover problem, and generic teaching would still need plant-specific follow-up before operators handle the new grader confidently.

Decision: SCR should choose on-the-job training initially, then fund short college modules for the most experienced operators. It is cheaper, directly relevant and avoids disrupting the 12,500-unit quarterly pack while defects stand at 3.3%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because the $6,300 and the loss of 9 of 30 staff would hurt delivery to wholesalers, and the course alone cannot teach SCR's exact grading settings.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with limited SCR context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in SCR's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in context with a justified decision on cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SCR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four applied uses: margin of safety of 20,000 units; average total cost of $8.60; labour productivity of about 1,667 units per worker; servicing the $300,000 loan.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($11.00 − $5.00) = $180,000 ÷ $6.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $11.00 − $5.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SCR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 30,000 units against output of 50,000 units gives a margin of safety of 20,000 units, showing how much fruit can be lost to the 3.3% blemish rate before losses occur.
2. Average total cost of $180,000 ÷ 50,000 + $5.00 = $8.60 a unit benchmarks packing costs and exposes waste.
3. Labour productivity of 50,000 units ÷ 30 staff = about 1,667 units a worker tests whether 11% turnover is affordable.
4. Contribution of $6.00 sets the sales volume needed to service the $300,000 bank loan used for the $540,000 shed.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCR's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SCR's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.46 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.70 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.73 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.06 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $70,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $190,000; 2025 current assets = $80,000 + $88,000 + $44,000 = $212,000. Dividing by $130,000 and $125,000 current liabilities gives 1.46 and 1.70. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($190,000 − $95,000) ÷ $130,000 = 0.73; 2025 = ($212,000 − $80,000) ÷ $125,000 = 1.06.

Evaluation: Both measures are better in 2025. The current ratio rose from 1.46 to 1.70 because current assets increased by $22,000 while current liabilities fell by $5,000, giving wholesalers and the bank more assurance. The acid test improving from 0.73 to 1.06 is the more meaningful evidence of real progress because it strips out inventories, which for perishable citrus may lose value if the 3.3% blemish rate is not controlled. Cash doubled from $25,000 to $44,000, giving SCR more room to meet seasonal bills while it services a $300,000 loan. The caveat is that trade receivables grew from $70,000 to $88,000, so cash is tied up with wholesalers, and a late payment would quickly weaken the ratios.

Conclusion: SCR's liquidity has clearly improved, and crucially the acid test now exceeds 1, so short-term debts can be met without relying on selling fruit stock. The remaining weakness is rising receivables, so tighter credit control with wholesalers is advisable before further spending on the $540,000 shed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little accurate ratio calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates both ratios for both years accurately with contextual comments on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios, evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities, and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SCR of promoting its citrus as locally grown.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Research of 400 buyers found 72% would pay up to $0.30 more for locally grown citrus and 58% check origin labels. A local-origin message can therefore support a price above $11.00, protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit against 10.2% fertiliser and packaging inflation and helping shift 50,000 units through national wholesalers. It also builds a distinctive identity for the partnership's new $540,000 packing shed.

Disadvantage: Stressing local origin limits the market to nearby buyers and may conflict with supplying national wholesalers, and the premium of $0.30 may not be accepted if shoppers cannot verify origin. The insert gives no breakdown of the $5.00 variable cost, so extra labelling or tracing costs cannot be quantified; if they raise unit cost, contribution falls. Any credibility problem with the 58% who check labels would also damage demand just as SCR faces 3.3% blemishes and 11% turnover.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using SCR's survey data and cost structure.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.2% rise in fertiliser and packaging input costs will affect SCR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): If the $300,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra cost is 0.75% × $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is small against $180,000 fixed costs and nil if the rate is fixed, though future borrowing for the $540,000 shed becomes dearer and consumers may reduce discretionary fruit spending. Fixing the rate would largely remove this risk.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.71 an hour): With a workforce of 30 this raises costs in packing and grading and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours or wage levels, so a valid annual total cannot be invented. The appropriate measure is productivity: 50,000 units ÷ 30 staff = about 1,667 units a worker, so the rise is bearable only if that productivity holds or output rises, otherwise unit labour cost eats into the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (10.2% fertiliser and packaging): The $5.00 variable cost is not decomposed, so only a bound can be computed: if all of it rose 10.2%, that is $0.51 a unit (0.102 × $5.00), or roughly $25,500 a year at 50,000 units. Even partial pass-through reduces contribution, but the $0.30 locally grown premium and 3.2% demand growth can offset part of it.

Conclusion: The 10.2% rise in fertiliser and packaging costs will have the greatest impact because it applies to every unit and directly reduces the $6.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 investment. The interest charge is a known $2,250, and the wage effect depends on unstated hours, while input inflation is broad and persistent and cannot be fixed by a single contract change.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited SCR application.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SCR's costs and finance in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes and concludes input-cost inflation has the greatest impact with reasons.
